articles.title: When your app gets a chat interface
articles.description: What happens after you hit Send? Try a small demo that puts chat and the records it finds side by side.
articles.body:
If I ask an app which requests are open, I want to see the rows it found. I might need to open one, check what’s going on, and get back to work. A paragraph can get me started. The record is where I pick up.

That’s the part of adding chat to an app I keep thinking about. We spend a lot of time on the answer. What can someone actually do with it?

## I’d keep the table

Say I’m looking for open requests in North. If I know where the filters are, I’ll use them. If I’m new to the app, I might just type “Show open records in North.” Either way, I should land on the same rows. If I meant South, let me change the filter right there.

In a real app, I’d have the model ask the app for those records. The server would check the filters and the user’s permissions, then fetch the rows through the same API the table uses. The reply can show the filters it used and give me links to the records I’m allowed to open.

## What if the record doesn’t say?

Say I open a request and ask why it’s still open. The row might only tell us the status. I’d show what the record says and say the reason isn’t recorded. Same thing if I ask what a repair costs and there’s no cost field.

I’d also try the whole thing with a keyboard. Can I submit a question, hear the reply with a screen reader, get to the source row, and find my way back? That’s the kind of test I’d run before shipping it.

## Try it here

Ask “Show open records in North,” open one of the rows, then ask what the repair will cost. The demo uses fictional records and runs on local rules. You can try the table filters too and see how they work alongside the conversation.

projects.title: Delano
projects.summary: A shared starting point for an Angular app. I wanted engineers to have somewhere to go for layouts and styles before building a screen from scratch.
projects.body:
## Why a shared kit?

When every screen starts from scratch, teams make the same layout and styling decisions over and over. A shared foundation gives people a place to start and makes the patterns easier to find later.

## What’s in the repository

The Delano README describes an application foundation with a layout module, shared styles, and a style-guide entry point. The project uses Angular and Less, with Nebular listed among its dependencies. There’s also a documentation command that uses Compodoc.

## What I’d take forward

I’d document the behavior alongside the visuals. For a component like a dialog, that means writing down what receives focus on open, how to close it, and where focus returns. The portfolio playground shows that idea in a small, separate example.
